seoTitle: How to Restore a Deleted Microsoft Loop Page
metaDescription: Recover an accidentally deleted Microsoft Loop page using the workspace trash bin, OneDrive, or SharePoint recycle bin recovery methods.
intro: Accidentally deleting a Loop page doesn't have to mean losing your work for good. Loop backs its pages with the same Microsoft 365 storage infrastructure as the rest of your tenant, which means a deleted page usually isn't actually gone — it's sitting in one of a few different trash locations depending on where the page lived. This guide walks through the workspace's own recycle bin first, since that's where most deletions land, then covers the OneDrive and SharePoint paths for pages tied to a private chat or a shared Teams channel.

steps.heading: Open your Loop workspace
steps.body: Sign in and land on the Loop home screen, which greets you with "Good Evening" (or the time-appropriate equivalent) above a grid of your workspaces — cards like "Workspace for Beginners" or "Workspace 101," each showing when it was last touched. Click into the specific workspace that contained the page you lost. Everything from here happens inside that workspace's own sidebar, not from this top-level home screen, so this is really just the jumping-off point.

image.caption: The Loop home screen listing available workspaces as cards, each timestamped with how recently it was opened.

steps.heading: Find the recycle bin at the bottom of the sidebar
steps.body: Once inside a workspace, the left sidebar lists your pages under "Sorted by hierarchy," the same list you use every day to navigate between pages. Scroll all the way to the bottom of that sidebar, below the last page in the list, and you'll find a Recycle bin link sitting on its own. It's easy to miss precisely because it's tucked at the very bottom rather than near the top-level navigation, but it's the first place to check for anything deleted from this specific workspace.

image.caption: A workspace sidebar with the page list under "Sorted by hierarchy" and the Recycle bin link visible at the very bottom.

steps.heading: Restore the page from the recycle bin
steps.body: Clicking Recycle bin opens a grid of everything recently deleted from that workspace. Hover over the missing page's title to reveal a three-dot menu, and choose Restore — the page pops back into the sidebar in roughly its original spot, with its content, tables, and components intact as of the moment it was deleted. This workspace-level recycle bin is the fastest recovery path and covers the vast majority of accidental deletions, so it's worth checking here before assuming a page needs a more involved recovery.

steps.heading: Check OneDrive for pages tied to a private chat
steps.body: Not every Loop page lives inside a shared workspace — pages created inside a one-on-one or small group chat are backed by your personal OneDrive rather than the workspace's shared storage. If a page you can't find in the workspace recycle bin was one you created inside a chat, open your Microsoft 365 OneDrive hub separately and check its own trash. Loop components created this way get stored as individual files there, so they're recovered the same way you'd recover any other accidentally deleted OneDrive file.

steps.heading: Check SharePoint for pages shared in a Teams channel
steps.body: Pages shared into a Teams channel are backed by that channel's connected SharePoint site instead of OneDrive. Open the channel's Files tab, jump into the associated SharePoint site, and open its recycle bin from there — deleted channel components typically show up in that SharePoint trash even when they don't appear in the workspace's own Recycle bin link. This is the path to try when a teammate reports a shared page is missing and neither of the first two locations turn it up.

steps.heading: Escalate to an IT admin for a fully deleted workspace
steps.body: If an entire workspace was deleted rather than a single page, none of the recovery paths above will help, since there's no sidebar left to check. In that case, the fastest route is your organization's IT admin, who can use the Microsoft 365 admin dashboard to restore a deleted workspace shell, provided the request comes in before the retention window closes — typically 93 days for a fully deleted workspace, after which recovery generally isn't possible at all.

steps.heading: Confirm the restored page is complete
steps.body: After any recovery path — workspace bin, OneDrive, or SharePoint — open the restored page and check that its tables, task lists, and any embedded components loaded back correctly rather than assuming a successful restore means everything came back intact. It's worth doing this check immediately rather than days later, since a partial restore is much easier to flag and fix while the deletion is still fresh in everyone's memory.

faq.question: How long do deleted Loop pages stay recoverable?
faq.answer: Deleted items typically stay in the recycle bin for a limited retention window, so it's best to restore a page as soon as you notice it's missing.

faq.question: Can I recover a page if the whole workspace was deleted?
faq.answer: In more serious cases, an IT admin may be able to use admin tools to recover a fully deleted workspace before the roughly 93-day retention window closes.

faq.question: Where do private Loop pages get stored when deleted?
faq.answer: Pages tied to individual chats are generally recoverable through your personal OneDrive trash rather than the shared workspace bin.

faq.question: Will restoring a page bring back its comments and tables?
faq.answer: Restoring a page from the recycle bin generally returns it to its last saved state, including its structured components, though it's worth double-checking after recovery.

faq.question: Why isn't a deleted page showing up in the workspace recycle bin?
faq.answer: If the page was created inside a private chat or shared through a Teams channel, it may be backed by OneDrive or SharePoint storage instead, so check those trash locations before assuming the page is unrecoverable.
